original_question: Find necessary and sufficient conditions on a general class of positive integer sequences so that, for a fixed n, there exist n distinct sequences from that class whose union covers all positive integers. In particular, for recurrence-defined classes Af = {(a_n) : a_n = f(a_{n-1},...,a_{n-i}) for n > i+1 with positive integer initial data}, determine when such covering is possible under the surjectivity-type conditions stated in the source.
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 31 ("On Crittenden and Vanden Eynden's Conjecture"), specifically the starred general question about when n distinct sequences from a class of positive-integer sequences cover all positive integers, together with Comment (b) introducing the recurrence-defined class A_f.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper's focus on covering the positive integers by unions of distinct sequences from a class, keeps the quantifier "for a fixed n," and correctly notices that the paper immediately specializes to recurrence-defined classes A_f and contrasts two image conditions on the defining map f.
missing_details: The exact source target is Unsolved Problem 31, not a standalone conjecture or theorem: it begins with the specific solved question about covering all positive integers by n geometric progressions, and then states the starred generalization.
The paper's ambient set is the positive integers; it first says "all (positive) integers," and later shortens this to "all integers."

The starred main question is: find necessary and sufficient conditions on a general class of positive-integer sequences such that, for a fixed n, there exist n distinct sequences from that class whose union covers all positive integers.

Comment (b) is only an example of such a class; it does not itself restate the fixed-n condition. It asks whether the whole class A_f covers all positive integers, so your draft slightly conflates the fixed-n main question with the later example.
In A_f, one must specify that i is a positive integer and that the initial data a_1, ..., a_i are arbitrary positive integers.
The recurrence index in the paper is n >= i + 1, not n > i + 1.
To make A_f stand alone, f should be stated as a map from i-tuples of positive integers to positive integers.

The first condition in Comment (b) is not merely a vague "surjectivity-type" condition: it is the exact omitted-value hypothesis that there exists y > 0 such that f(x_1, ..., x_i) != y for every positive-integer input tuple.

The paper then explicitly contrasts this with the surjectivity condition that for every y > 0 there exists a positive-integer input tuple with f(x_1, ..., x_i) = y, and says that under this changed condition the answer is generally negative.

The source also gives a solved negative example for geometric progressions: no finite union of integer geometric progressions can cover all positive integers, by choosing a prime outside the finite set of first terms and ratios.
refined_question: For a fixed positive integer n, find necessary and sufficient conditions on a class C of sequences of positive integers such that there exist n distinct sequences in C whose union is the set of all positive integers. As the concrete example singled out in the paper, let i be a positive integer, let f map i-tuples of positive integers to positive integers, and let A_f be the class of all sequences (a_n)_{n>=1} with arbitrary positive initial values a_1, ..., a_i and recurrence a_n = f(a_{n-1}, ..., a_{n-i}) for every n >= i + 1. Under the hypothesis that f omits some positive integer value, i.e. there exists y > 0 such that f(x_1, ..., x_i) != y for every positive-integer tuple (x_1, ..., x_i), does the class A_f cover all positive integers? The paper further notes that if this hypothesis is replaced by surjectivity of f on the positive integers, then in general the answer is no.
justification: The draft is clearly aimed at Unsolved Problem 31 rather than any other item in the paper: its first sentence matches the starred general problem on classes of positive-integer sequences, and its second sentence matches the immediately following example A_f in Comment (b). The paper also supplies nearby context that must be retained for fidelity: Comment (a) gives the negative answer for geometric progressions, while Comment (b) defines A_f, states the exact omitted-value condition on f, and then contrasts it with the surjectivity condition, which the author says is generally insufficient. Those are the paper-faithful details needed to sharpen the draft into a stand-alone question.
